newsitem.title: USA: House panel says no U.S. funds for assisted suicide.
newsitem.headline: House panel says no U.S. funds for assisted suicide.

text.p: A U.S. House panel voted Thursday to block any federal health funds from paying for assisted suicides, a divisive moral issue that U.S. courts and state governments are wrestling with.

Should assisted suicide become legal, the bill would ensure that Medicare, Medicaid, veteran's health, Indian health and public health dollars not pay for it. Federal funds are not now used for such deaths.
The House Commerce committee vote was 44-2, with two Democrats dissenting. One of them, California Democrat Henry Waxman, said the bill was "sanctimonious" and unnecessary.
"It's premature and will curb our society's debate over assisted suicide," Waxman said.
The bill is likely to be brought before the full House in early April. "It will pass overwhelmingly," predicted Commerce committee chairman Thomas Bliley, a Virginia Republican.
The Senate has not started working on a similar bill.
The Clinton administration has opposed assisted-suicide, and argued against it in a landmark right-to-die case now pending in the Supreme Court.

Proponents of physician-assisted suicides say mentally-competent, terminally ill patients should have the right to end their life when it becomes unbearable. Critics, including many major medical groups, say it is morally unacceptable for doctors to end the lives of their patients.
More than 40 states have outlawed assisted suicide. An Oregon measure that would allow it is tied up in court.

If a state did legalize assisted suicide, the bill would not block it from using its own funds under Medicaid, which is a state-federal health program. But it could not use any of the federal portion.
The bill does not outlaw assisted suicide, or dictate whether private health plans can pay for it.

Nor does the bill interfere with a terminally ill patient's right to refuse further treatment, such as chemotherapy, or to refuse food, water, or other care. It does not limit a patient's access to medicine for pain.

In largely party line votes, the committee defeated two Democratic-sponsored amendments. One would have withheld some medical education funds if medical schools do not improve their education about end of life care. The other called for a federal health agency to set up guidelines for palliative care and pain management for the dying.

The bill does call for a one-year study of medical school curricula in this area, and it sets up some pilot programs for education. Across the political spectrum, and throughout the medical community, there is a widespread belief that medical schools are not adequately preparing doctors to treat intractible pain or to help patients at the end of life.
